es.q: Discuss the pathology and common sites of spread of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma as outlined in the study notes.
es.m:
- **Ductal adenocarcinoma proportion:** Accounts for about 80% of pancreatic neoplasms, arising from the duct epithelium.
- **Spread at diagnosis:** More than 85% have spread beyond the gland at the time of diagnosis.
- **Invasion characteristics:** Features early perineural invasion and lymphatic spread.
- **Common metastatic sites:** The commonest sites of distant disease are the liver and peritoneum, followed by the lungs.
- **Anatomical location:** About 75% occur in the head of the pancreas, and 25% occur in the body and tail.
es.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: Essay quest

ai.clinicalScope: Invasive adenocarcinoma arising from glandular epithelium in adult patients presenting to East African and other low‑resource hospitals, with emphasis on the most common sites (lung, colorectal, gastric, cervix, breast).
ai.title: Adenocarcinoma Overview
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Adenocarcinoma is a cancer that starts in cells that make glands or secrete substances. It can affect many organs; in low‑resource settings the most frequent sites are the lung, colon, stomach, cervix and breast.

sections.p: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumour composed of cells that form gland‑like structures and produce mucin or other secretions. It is classified by organ of origin and by histologic grade (well, moderately, poorly differentiated).
b: Invasive glands with loss of polarity
Mucin production detectable with PAS or mucicarmine stains
Immunohistochemistry (CK7, CK20, CDX2, ER, HER2) helps locate the primary site
Grades 1‑3 reflect differentiation and correlate with prognosis

sections.p: Risk factors vary by organ but share themes of chronic irritation, infection, and environmental exposures common in low‑resource settings.
b: Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection → gastric adenocarcinoma
Biomass fuel smoke exposure → lung adenocarcinoma in non‑smokers, especially women
Schistosoma haematobium infection (rare) → bladder adenocarcinoma
Human papillomavirus (HPV) 16/18 → cervical adenocarcinoma
HIV‑related immunosuppression → earlier colorectal adenocarcinoma
Diet low in fruits/vegetables, high in smoked/processed foods → gastric and colorectal cancers

sections.p: Carcinogenesis proceeds through genetic and epigenetic alterations that drive uncontrolled glandular proliferation and invasion.
b: Chronic inflammation → DNA damage (e.g., H. pylori → CagA‑mediated p53 loss)
Activation of oncogenes (KRAS, EGFR) and loss of tumour suppressors (APC, TP53)
Acquisition of hallmarks: self‑sufficiency in growth signals, evasion of apoptosis, angiogenesis
Epithelial‑mesenchymal transition (EMT) enables invasion and metastasis
Mucin over‑production creates a protective microenvironment

sections.p: Macroscopically, adenocarcinomas appear as irregular, firm masses that may ulcerate or infiltrate surrounding tissue.
b: Lung: peripheral, tan‑white nodules, often with necrotic centre
Colon: ulcerated polypoid lesion, may cause obstruction
Stomach: thickened wall with an ulcerated or infiltrative appearance
Cervix: exophytic or ulcerated mass on the endocervical canal
Breast: ill‑defined, firm, often with skin dimpling

sections.p: Histology shows glandular formation, mucin, and varying degrees of cellular atypia.
b: Well‑differentiated: tall columnar cells, preserved polarity, abundant mucin
Moderately differentiated: irregular glands, nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses
Poorly differentiated: solid sheets, loss of gland formation, necrosis
Special stains: PAS/DAB for mucin, Alcian blue for acidic mucins
Immunoprofile guides site: CK7+/CK20‑ (lung, breast), CK7‑/CK20+ (colorectal), CDX2+ (colorectal), ER+/PR+ (breast)

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the organ involved and the tumour’s local or metastatic effects.
b: Lung: persistent cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, pleural effusion
Colorectal: change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, obstruction
Gastric: epigastric pain, early satiety, anemia, occult bleeding
Cervical: post‑coital bleeding, pelvic pain, abnormal discharge
Breast: palpable lump, skin retraction, nipple discharge

sections.p: Diagnosis relies on tissue confirmation and staging investigations; when a test is unavailable, clinical judgment and alternative modalities are used.

t.b: Confirms malignant glandular cells and grade – required for any definitive diagnosis
Detects peripheral mass or pleural effusion – suggests lung primary
Identifies mass, organomegaly, ascites – useful when CT not accessible
Monitors treatment response; elevated >5 ng/mL may support colorectal/gastric origin

t.a: Immunohistochemistry panel (CK7, CK20, CDX2, ER, HER2)
t.b: Helps locate primary when metastasis is first presentation

sections.p: Staging follows the TNM system (Tumour size/extent, Node involvement, Metastasis) specific to each organ; grading is histologic.
b: T1‑T4 based on depth of invasion (e.g., colorectal T1 = submucosa, T4 = serosa or adjacent organ)
N0‑N2 based on number and location of regional lymph nodes
M0 vs M1 distinguishes resectable from metastatic disease
Stage I‑IV integrates TNM; higher stage predicts poorer survival
Grade 1 (well) → better prognosis; Grade 3 (poor) → aggressive behaviour

sections.p: Complications arise from local invasion, metastasis, and treatment side‑effects.
b: Obstructive jaundice (pancreatic/ biliary adenocarcinoma)
Intestinal obstruction or perforation (colorectal)
Superior vena cava syndrome (lung)
Hypercalcaemia from bone metastases
Cachexia and anemia worsen functional status
Five‑year survival varies: lung ~15 %, colorectal ~60 % (stage‑dependent), gastric ~30 %

sections.p: Management combines curative surgery, systemic therapy, and supportive care, adapted to resource availability.
b: Surgery with negative margins is first‑line for resectable disease
Adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., platinum‑based for lung, fluoropyrimidine‑based for colorectal) improves survival
Targeted therapy (EGFR, HER2) only when molecular testing is feasible
Radiotherapy for local control (e.g., cervical, rectal) when surgery not possible
Palliative care: analgesia, nutritional support, management of effusions

sections.p: Linking morphology with clinical behaviour guides management decisions.
b: Well‑differentiated tumours often present earlier and are surgically resectable
Poorly differentiated tumours have higher nodal involvement and need systemic therapy
Mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon may present with mucin‑filled ascites (pseudomyxoma peritonei)
HPV‑positive cervical adenocarcinoma responds better to radiotherapy
Biomass‑related lung adenocarcinoma often harbours EGFR mutations, influencing targeted therapy choice

sections.p: When faced with a suspected adenocarcinoma, follow a systematic bedside and investigative pathway.
b: Take focused history: organ‑specific symptoms, risk exposures (smoking, biomass, infections)
Perform targeted exam: auscultate lungs, palpate abdomen, inspect breast/cervix
Order tissue diagnosis first; if unavailable, use imaging and tumour markers to guide urgent referral
Stage disease before committing to curative surgery
Discuss multidisciplinary plan: surgery, chemo, radiotherapy, palliative care

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe dyspnoea or massive hemoptysis
Rapidly rising bilirubin with right‑upper‑quadrant pain (obstructive jaundice)
Unexplained high‑grade fever with neutropenia after chemotherapy

faq.q: Is every glandular tumour an adenocarcinoma?
faq.a: Only malignant tumours that form invasive glands are called adenocarcinomas; benign glandular proliferations are adenomas.

faq.q: Can adenocarcinoma be cured without surgery?
faq.a: In early‑stage disease (e.g., T1N0) some organ sites (e.g., early gastric) may be treated with endoscopic resection, but surgery remains the main curative option.
It identifies the tissue of origin when the primary tumour is unknown, guiding appropriate treatment.

exam: A 45‑year‑old woman with chronic biomass fuel exposure presents with a peripheral lung mass and cough. Which molecular test would you request and why? — EGFR mutation analysis; positive result guides EGFR‑TKI therapy, especially in non‑smokers.

A patient from a rural clinic has occult blood on stool testing and a 3‑cm ulcerated colonic lesion on sigmoidoscopy. What is the next step in staging? — Perform CT of abdomen/pelvis and chest to assess T, N, and M status before surgery.

During a breast exam you find a firm, ill‑defined mass with skin dimpling. Core biopsy shows poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, ER‑negative, HER2‑positive. What systemic therapy is indicated? — HER2‑targeted therapy (trastuzumab) combined with chemotherapy; avoid hormonal therapy because ER‑negative.

A 60‑year‑old man with known gastric adenocarcinoma develops new ascites. Cytology shows malignant cells. How does this finding alter management? — Indicates peritoneal metastasis (M1), shifting treatment from curative surgery to palliative chemotherapy.

Explain why a high serum CEA is not diagnostic of colorectal cancer in low‑resource settings. — CEA can be elevated in smoking, inflammation, and other cancers; it is only useful for monitoring after tissue diagnosis.

A patient with HIV presents with weight loss and a right‑sided colonic mass. What additional infection‑related risk should you consider? — Chronic infection with human papillomavirus or EBV can accelerate colorectal carcinogenesis in immunosuppressed hosts.

You have only an ultrasound available. How can you use it to differentiate a hepatic adenocarcinoma metastasis from a benign hemangioma? — Look for irregular margins, heterogeneous echotexture, and rapid wash‑out on Doppler; hemangioma shows well‑defined, peripheral nodular enhancement.
During a cervical screening a biopsy shows glandular atypia. Which HPV genotype testing is most relevant? — HPV 16 and 18, as they are most strongly linked to cervical adenocarcinoma.

A patient with stage III colon cancer is planned for adjuvant therapy but lacks access to oxaliplatin. What alternative regimen can be used? — Fluoropyrimidine (5‑FU) based therapy alone, acknowledging slightly lower efficacy.

What are the red‑flag signs that require urgent referral for a suspected lung adenocarcinoma? — Massive hemoptysis, new-onset severe dyspnoea, pleural effusion causing respiratory compromise, and rapid weight loss.
